related_questions.question: Are rabies an infectious disease?
related_questions.snippet: Rabies is a deadly virus spread to people from the saliva of infected animals. The rabies virus is usually transmitted through a bite. Animals most likely to transmit rabies in the United States include bats, coyotes, foxes, raccoons and skunks.

related_questions.question: Can rabies be spread from person to person?

text_blocks.snippet: No, rabies is not typically spread from person to person. The virus is almost always transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. While rare, human-to-human transmission has been documented in a few instances through corneal and solid organ transplants.
snippet_highlighted_words: No, rabies is not typically spread from person to person

list.title: Animal Bites are the Main Route:
list.snippet: Rabies is primarily spread through the saliva of infected animals, usually through bites or scratches.

list.title: Rare Human-to-Human Transmission:
list.snippet: There are very few documented cases of human-to-human rabies transmission. These cases have primarily occurred through corneal and solid organ transplants.

list.title: No Evidence for Other Transmission:
list.snippet: There is no evidence that rabies can be spread through casual contact, like touching a person with rabies or contact with their urine, blood, or feces.

list.title: Healthcare Workers at Minimal Risk:
list.snippet: Healthcare workers caring for patients with rabies do not pose a significant risk to their families or communities, as long as they take standard precautions and avoid contact with infectious fluids.

list.title: Importance of Post-Exposure Prophylaxis:
list.snippet: If someone is exposed to rabies through a bite or scratch, prompt post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is crucial to prevent the disease.

list.title: Risk Assessment:
list.snippet: If you are concerned about a potential rabies exposure, it is important to consult with a healthcare professional for a risk assessment and appropriate treatment.

related_questions.question: What is the mode of transmission of rabies?

text_blocks.snippet: Rabies is primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected animal. The rabies virus is present in the saliva of infected animals and can enter a new host through a bite wound. While bites are the most common route, other forms of exposure, such as scratches, open wounds, or mucous membranes (like the mouth or eyes) contaminated with infected saliva or nervous tissue, can also transmit the virus. Person-to-person transmission is extremely rare and has only been documented through tissue or organ transplantation.
snippet_highlighted_words: primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected animal

list.title: Bites:
list.snippet: Traumatic bites that puncture the skin are the highest risk for rabies transmission. However, even low-trauma bites like nips from young animals or bats can lead to infection.

list.title: Non-bite exposures:
list.snippet: Scratches, abrasions, and open wounds contaminated with saliva or nervous tissue can also transmit the virus.

list.title: Mucous membranes:
list.snippet: Contact with infected saliva or nervous tissue entering mucous membranes (like the mouth, eyes, or genitalia) can also lead to infection.

list.title: Inhalation:
list.snippet: Inhalation of aerosolized rabies virus is a potential route of exposure, but this is primarily a concern for laboratory workers who handle the virus.

list.title: Rare routes:
list.snippet: Other types of contact, like petting a rabid animal or contact with their blood, urine, or feces, do not typically lead to infection.
